column1: What does \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) mean in plain words?
column2: As x gets close to a (but not equal to a), f(x) gets as close to L as you like.

column1: Does the value f(a) affect \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\)?
column2: No. The limit only looks at inputs near a, never at a itself.

column1: You substitute and get 0/0. What next?
column2: Simplify first: factor and cancel, or multiply by a conjugate. 0/0 is a signal, not an answer.

column1: When does a two-sided limit exist?
column2: When the left limit and the right limit both exist and are equal.

column1: State the epsilon-delta definition of a limit.
column2: For every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) with \(0 < |x-a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\).

column1: Three conditions for continuity at a
column2: f(a) exists, the limit at a exists, and they are equal.

column1: Name the three kinds of discontinuity.

column2: If f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs, f has a zero between a and b.

column1: Which everyday SRE tool is the Intermediate Value Theorem in action?
column2: git bisect: a pass and a later fail guarantee a first bad commit in between.
